milestones.title: Roman conquest; Lutetia founded
milestones.detail: Caesar's general Labienus defeats the Parisii at the Battle of Lutetia in 52 BCE; a Roman town is then begun on the Left Bank, centred on a forum atop the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève.

milestones.title: Germanic invasions shrink the city
milestones.detail: From 275 Germanic raids drive residents from the Left Bank to the Île de la Cité, which is walled with stone from abandoned monuments: the first city wall of Paris.

milestones.title: Clovis makes Paris his capital
milestones.detail: Clovis I, first king of the Merovingian dynasty, makes the city his capital from 508.

milestones.title: Viking siege
milestones.detail: Paris withstands a Viking siege in 885-886, establishing its strategic importance; its defender, Count Odo, is later elected king of West Francia.

milestones.title: Wall of Philip Augustus
milestones.detail: Before leaving on the Third Crusade, Philip II orders a stone wall to protect the capital; it is built from 1190 to 1213, with the Louvre fortress just outside its western limit.

milestones.title: The Black Death
milestones.detail: In the first plague epidemic of 1348-1349 forty to fifty thousand Parisians die, about a quarter of the population; the plague returns repeatedly.

milestones.title: Wall of Charles V and the Bastille
milestones.detail: Between 1356 and 1383 Charles V builds a new wall of fortifications and the Bastille, a fortress guarding the Porte Saint-Antoine at the eastern end of the city.

milestones.title: Storming of the Bastille
milestones.detail: Parisians storm the Bastille on 14 July 1789, at the outbreak of the French Revolution; the fortress is demolished in 1789-1790.

milestones.title: Thiers wall
milestones.detail: The last defensive wall of Paris, a 33 km circuit of wall and ditch around the city of the July Monarchy, is built between 1841 and 1846.

milestones.title: Haussmann's renovation begins
milestones.detail: Between 1853 and 1870 Napoleon III's prefect Haussmann cuts wide boulevards through the old city and builds new parks, sewers, aqueducts and a central market.

milestones.title: Suburbs annexed; twenty arrondissements
milestones.detail: Napoleon III annexes the surrounding towns and creates eight new arrondissements, expanding Paris to its present limits.

milestones.title: Siege of Paris and the Commune
milestones.detail: Prussian-led forces besiege the city from 19 September 1870 to 28 January 1871; the revolutionary Paris Commune then holds power from 18 March to 28 May 1871.

milestones.title: Universal Exposition and the Eiffel Tower
milestones.detail: The 1889 exposition, marking the centennial of the Revolution, features the new 300 m Eiffel Tower.

milestones.title: Métro opens
milestones.detail: The first Métro line, Porte Maillot to Porte de Vincennes, is inaugurated on 19 July 1900 during the World's Fair.

milestones.title: Liberation of Paris
milestones.detail: The German-occupied city is liberated on 25 August 1944 by the French 2nd Armoured Division and the US 4th Infantry Division.

milestones.title: Summer Olympic Games
milestones.detail: Paris hosts the Summer Olympics for the third time, after 1900 and 1924.

notes: Start date is contested. The Parisii lived in the area from about the middle of the 3rd century BCE, but the site of their oppidum is disputed (the Île de la Cité, or a large Gallic settlement excavated at Nanterre), so the start is set at 52 BCE, when Caesar's account documents Lutetia and the Roman town was founded; using the Parisii settlement instead would put the start around 250 BCE. Population: nothing was found for the Gallic period; the single Roman-era figure (6,000-8,000) is from one historian, and there is no estimate between it and 800. The Wikipedia table's uncited figures of 25,000 (59 BCE) and 80,000 (150 CE) were not used. Points for 800-1750 are Chandler's estimates (via Reba et al.). Medieval Paris is strongly contested: Chandler gives 274,000 for 1328 and Wikipedia's 'Paris in the Middle Ages' two hundred thousand, while the dataset 'The Population of European Cities from 700 to 2000' (Research Data Journal for the Humanities and Social Sciences, 2021, https://doi.org/10.1163/24523666-06010003, read via the Wikipedia table) gives 15,000 (1000), 44,000 (1200), 75,000 (1300), 54,000 (1400), 94,000 (1500), 300,000 (1600), 500,000 (1700). 1801-1861 are census counts for the City of Paris (1861 within the enlarged limits of 1860). From 1863 the series switches to urban-area (agglomeration) estimates so that it joins the UN series; the rounded values for 1863, 1885 and 1905 mark when the agglomeration passed 2, 3 and 4 million. City-proper censuses after 1861, not used in the series, were 1,825,274 (1866), 1,851,792 (1872, after the siege and Commune), 1,988,806 (1876), 2,269,023 (1881), 2,344,550 (1886), 2,447,957 (1891), 2,536,834 (1896), 2,714,068 (1901), 2,763,393 (1906), 2,888,110 (1911), 2,906,472 (1921, the city's peak), 2,871,429 (1926), 2,891,020 (1931), 2,829,753 (1936), 2,725,374 (1946). Landmarks: modern towers from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center (La Défense towers are listed there under Courbevoie and Puteaux; Tour First was first completed in 1974 and its 2011 date is the end of a 2007-2011 renovation that gave it its present height; The Link is listed as completed in 2026). Older monuments are from Wikipedia articles and marked estimated where the article gives no primary citation. Notre-Dame is entered at its tower height; its 19th-century spire, destroyed in the 2019 fire and since rebuilt, is taller but no sourced figure was recorded. Left out for lack of a sourced height: Arènes de Lutèce and Thermes de Cluny (Roman), Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Sainte-Chapelle (only the 33 m spire is given), the Louvre and Tuileries palaces, Palais Garnier, Basilica of Saint-Denis, Stade de France.
